title: Microtask Starvation Guard & Fair Task Scheduler
problemStatement: If recursive microtasks continually schedule more microtasks, the event loop locks up and macrotasks/UI renders never run. Implement `fairScheduler(tasks, maxMicrotasksPerYield)` that executes tasks via microtasks, but yields to a macrotask (`setTimeout`) after `maxMicrotasksPerYield` tasks to prevent UI starvation.
interviewTrap: Infinite microtasks (`while(true) queueMicrotask(...)`) cause complete page freeze because the event loop will never leave the microtask checkpoint to service browser renders or user clicks.

testCases.name: Processes large batch correctly with yields
testCases.testFn: const tasks = Array.from({ length: 10 }, (_, i) => () => i); const res = await fairScheduler(tasks, 3); return res.length;

testCases.name: Allows interleaved macrotask execution during yields
testCases.testFn: let timerFired = false; setTimeout(() => { timerFired = true; }, 0); const tasks = Array.from({ length: 8 }, () => () => 1); await fairScheduler(tasks, 2); return timerFired;

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: Because the event loop drains the microtask queue until it is completely empty before running any macrotask or browser rendering, recursively queueing microtasks causes *Microtask Starvation* (freezing the UI and starving I/O). A Fair Task Scheduler interleaves large batches by voluntarily yielding to the macrotask queue or scheduler API.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Process items in slices (chunk size, e.g. 10 items).
If remaining items exist, check elapsed time or chunk limit.
Yield control to the macrotask queue using `await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 0))` or `scheduler.yield()`.
This allows interleaved macrotasks (user input, timeouts, UI rendering) to execute before resuming the batch.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: The browser renders frames (requestAnimationFrame and Paint) between macrotask turns.Draining microtasks without yielding blocks the main thread completely. Yielding to a macrotask gives the browser event loop opportunity to process the UI and other tasks.

complexity.time: O(N) total processing time for N items.
complexity.space: O(N) memory for queued task items.

edgeCasesHandled: Interleaving allows macrotasks scheduled concurrently to execute.
Large tasks (e.g. 1,000 items) finish completely without freezing the thread.
Graceful completion on empty or single-item queues.

specifications: W3C Scheduling APIs: scheduler.yield() and Prioritized Task Scheduling
HTML Living Standard §8.1.6.2 Processing model (Macrotask vs Microtask starvation risks)
verifiedRules: Microtasks starve macrotasks if chained infinitely without yield.
Yielding via setTimeout(0) or scheduler.yield breaks synchronous task monopolization.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: How does scheduler.yield() in modern browsers improve upon setTimeout(0) for task interleaving?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: `scheduler.yield()` (W3C Prioritized Task Scheduling API) yields control back to the browser to process high-priority input (clicks, keypresses) and rendering, but immediately resumes the yielded task ahead of lower-priority macrotasks. Unlike `setTimeout(0)`, it avoids the 4ms clamping penalty and preserves task priority inheritance.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Tests cutting-edge web performance knowledge and familiarity with modern W3C standards.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Why does long-running JavaScript cause dropped frames (jank)?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: At 60Hz, the browser must render a new frame every 16.6ms (at 120Hz, every 8.3ms). Because JavaScript execution runs on the exact same main thread as style recalculation, layout, and painting, any JavaScript task that runs longer than ~5ms risks blocking the render step, resulting in a dropped frame and visible animation stutter.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Connects JavaScript execution times directly to web performance metrics (INP / FID).

realWorldUseCases.description: React's Scheduler chunks large component trees into 5ms slices using `MessageChannel.port1.postMessage`, yielding to the browser between chunks to keep the page responsive.
Monaco Editor and Prism.js chunk tokenization of 100,000-line files across multiple animation frames to prevent editor UI freezing.

howToExplain.opening: A Fair Task Scheduler breaks long synchronous computations into small time slices, voluntarily yielding the thread back to the event loop to allow user inputs and rendering to interleave.
keyPoints: Monopolizing the main thread causes microtask starvation and input latency.
Chunking tasks with a ~5ms frame budget preserves 60fps responsiveness.
Yielding can be accomplished via MessageChannel, scheduler.yield(), or setTimeout(0).
React Fiber and browser editors rely on this pattern to perform massive computations without freezing the tab.
howToExplain.closingImpression: Writing code that plays nicely with the browser's render pipeline is what separates senior frontend engineers from average developers.
analogies: Like letting a person with one item cut ahead of you at the grocery register when you have three full shopping carts.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using requestAnimationFrame to yield long tasks.
commonMistakes.why: rAF is synchronized with the display refresh rate (16ms) and runs BEFORE paint. Calling rAF in a processing loop throttles throughput to 60 items per second.
commonMistakes.correct: Use MessageChannel or scheduler.yield() which yield to the macrotask queue without waiting for display v-sync.

followUpDeepDive.question: Why did React choose MessageChannel over setTimeout(0) for its scheduler polyfill?
followUpDeepDive.answer: `setTimeout(0)` has a 4ms clamp after 5 nested calls and prioritizes timer wheel bookkeeping. `MessageChannel.port1.postMessage` schedules an immediate macrotask without the 4ms clamp, providing near-instant thread resumption while still yielding to inputs and rendering.
